passage: Siddharth, you remind me of myself at fifteen, so listen. Your Jaya Dadi was the maths girl of her class. One evening before the exam, my friend Meenal came over with her geometry book and asked me to explain circle theorems. I rattled it off: "Angle at centre is double, so this is sixty, cyclic quad, opposite angles, done." I jumped over every line in between, because to me they were plain as daylight. Meenal kept nodding, "Hmm, hmm, okay." I felt so clever. The next day she showed me her paper. The same question, left blank. She said, "I didn't want to look slow in front of you." That stung. I had forgotten that I too once stared at those circles as if they were a foreign alphabet. After that, I drew every step on paper and stopped to say, "Now you write the next line."

qa.q: What did Meenal bring when she came over?
qa.a: Meenal came over with her geometry book and asked Jaya to explain circle theorems.

qa.q: How did Jaya feel while explaining, and how did that change the next day?
qa.a: Jaya felt clever and pleased while rattling off the answer, then stung and guilty on seeing Meenal's blank paper.

qa.q: What could young Jaya have done that evening to be sure Meenal understood?
qa.a: Jaya could have drawn each step, said why it followed, and asked Meenal to write the next line herself instead of trusting the nods.

qa.q: What was the lesson like for Meenal?
qa.a: For Meenal it was confusing and a little embarrassing; she nodded because she did not want to look slow, and then could not answer that question in the exam.

grounding: Shows a teenager explaining too fast with class shorthand while a friend nods along without understanding.

passage: Avni, you asked why I still keep that old chemistry notebook. At nineteen, in my second year of college, I tutored a first-year boy, Karthik, in organic chemistry. I thought I knew it cold; I had topped the paper. In the first week he asked, "But why does the electron move this way and not that way?" I opened my mouth and nothing came. I had memorised the arrows, never the reason. That night I sat up with my textbook, the way I should have done in first year. Every Tuesday he brought a new "but why", and every Tuesday I found another hole in my own head. So I started writing each explanation in this notebook before our sessions and testing it on my roommate first. By the end of term Karthik passed well, and honestly, so did my own understanding. Your Farida Khala learned more from those Tuesdays than from any lecture.

qa.q: What did Farida do before each session with Karthik?
qa.a: She wrote each explanation in her notebook and tested it on her roommate first.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling when Karthik first asked why the electron moves that way?
qa.a: Farida felt caught out and embarrassed, because she had topped the paper yet found she had memorised the arrows without knowing the reason.

qa.q: Which choice in the story turned Farida's weak spot into real understanding?
qa.a: Sitting up with the textbook to find the reason, then writing and testing each explanation before sessions, turned every question into a chance to fill a gap.

qa.q: How might Karthik have experienced being tutored by Farida?
qa.a: Karthik had a tutor who took his "but why" questions seriously and came back with clearer answers each week, which helped him pass well.

grounding: Shows a student tutoring a junior and finding gaps in their own understanding as the junior's questions arrive.

passage:
"Pivot table. Rows, values, filter. Got it?" Maria's cursor was already moving.
"Sorry, which column goes in rows?"
Maria sighed. "Region, Suraj. I showed you this yesterday."
"Right. Yes."
"And sales go in values. Obviously."
Suraj nodded. He had no idea why his totals kept looking wrong.
"Any questions?"
He had three. "No, it's clear."
"Good. Regional sheet by four."
At four he sent it. Ten minutes later a message came: "You've counted instead of summed. Did you listen at all?"
"I'll fix it," he typed.
At his desk he searched a video site for "pivot table basics" and watched with the sound at the lowest setting, angling the screen away from the aisle.
Across the aisle, Nikhil leaned over. "She talks to everyone like that. Ask me next time, no sighing, promise."
Suraj gave a small, tired laugh. "Okay. Thanks."

qa.q: What mistake did Maria find in Suraj's sheet?
qa.a: He had counted instead of summed.

qa.q: Why did Suraj say "No, it's clear" when he had three questions?
qa.a: Suraj felt slow and embarrassed after Maria's sighs and her "Obviously", so he was afraid another question would bring more scorn.

qa.q: How could Maria explain the next task so Suraj keeps asking?
qa.a: She could slow down, say why each column goes where it does, and invite questions without sighing, perhaps letting him build one step while she watches.

qa.q: How does Nikhil see what is happening to Suraj?
qa.a: Nikhil sees it as Maria's habit, not Suraj's failing, and offers to be someone Suraj can ask without being made to feel stupid.

grounding: Shows a learner taught with contempt by an impatient expert who stops asking questions and pretends to follow.

passage:
Tuesday night.
Rehana's third day at the bakery. Yesterday I explained proofing for ten minutes and she nodded through all of it, then left the trays too close to the oven and the dough went slack. My fault as much as hers.
Today I tried it differently. First I asked what she already knew. "I make rotis at home. I let the atta rest." Perfect, so I began there: resting roti dough and proofing bread are cousins, both need time, only here it's more warmth and more time.
One example only. I pressed a finger into a risen bun and showed her how the dent springs back halfway, slowly.
Then I asked her to tell it back to me. She said, "It's ready when it pushes back a bit. Not fully, not never." Better than my version!
Then the real test: she checked the second tray alone. Called it right 🙂
Note to self: nodding means nothing. The tray tells the truth.
Jaya

qa.q: What did Rehana say she does at home?
qa.a: She makes rotis at home and lets the atta rest.

qa.q: How did Jaya feel about the first day's explanation?
qa.a: Jaya felt guilty and partly to blame, writing "My fault as much as hers" after ten minutes of nodding hid that Rehana had not understood.

qa.q: Which steps in Jaya's new approach worked, and why?
qa.a: Starting from Rehana's roti dough, giving one finger-press example, asking her to say it back, and letting her check a tray alone showed whether it had really landed.

qa.q: What might the second day have been like for Rehana?
qa.a: Rehana probably felt more confident, because the lesson began with something she knew and she got to prove it by judging the tray herself.

grounding: Shows an explainer starting from what the learner knows, using one example, and checking understanding with a small real task.

subtype: Parent or elder teaching a skill [Observer]
passage:
Trisha was restocking thread at the community centre's Saturday tailoring class when she noticed the corner table. Lalremsiami, the oldest teacher there, sat beside a teenage boy, Deepu, who was fighting a jammed sewing machine. The thread had knotted under the plate. Trisha's hands itched; she knew the fix and half-rose from her stool.
Lalremsiami didn't move. She sipped her tea and asked only, "Where does the thread go after the needle?"
Deepu muttered, pulled the bobbin out, frowned, and put it back the wrong way. Trisha winced. Another minute passed.
"Look at the little arrow," Lalremsiami said, tapping the machine once.
Deepu turned the bobbin, rethreaded, and pressed the pedal. The needle ran clean. He grinned and sewed a whole seam without looking up.
Trisha sat back down, a little embarrassed at how fast she had wanted to grab it.

qa.q: What had gone wrong with Deepu's sewing machine?
qa.a: It was jammed; the thread had knotted under the plate.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling as she watched Deepu struggle?
qa.a: Trisha felt restless and tense, itching to fix it herself, and afterwards a little embarrassed at how fast she had wanted to grab it.

qa.q: What small step did Lalremsiami use to help without taking over?
qa.a: She waited, asked one question, and only after Deepu had tried for a while gave a single hint by tapping the little arrow.

qa.q: How might Deepu feel after getting the machine running himself?
qa.a: Deepu likely felt proud and more confident; he grinned and sewed a whole seam after solving it with only small hints.

grounding: Shows an observer watching an elder let a young person struggle a little before offering a small hint.

subtype: Group project where parts do not fit [Observer]
passage:
I'm Bidisha, and I share a hostel room with Urmila, so I watched the whole thing from my bed. Her group of three had split the robotics project two weeks earlier: Urmila wrote the sensor code, Rohan built the motor board, Aarti made the chassis. They met again only the night before the demo.
Around eleven the laptop was plugged in and the robot sat on our floor. It jerked forward and crashed into my cupboard. Urmila's code sent distances in centimetres; Rohan's board expected metres. Then Aarti's chassis turned out to be too narrow for Rohan's battery.
Nobody shouted, but nobody said much either. Urmila kept rubbing her eyes. Rohan said, "I thought we'd agreed on metres," and Urmila said, "When?"
They worked till three with tape and a converted number. I can't say what each of them was thinking. I only know one short test run in the first week would have shown all of it.

qa.q: What unit did Rohan's board expect?
qa.a: Rohan's board expected metres.

qa.q: What does Bidisha's account suggest about how Bidisha felt watching the group that night?
qa.a: Bidisha seems concerned and a little helpless, quietly noticing the silence and Urmila rubbing her eyes while admitting not knowing what each of them was thinking.

qa.q: What could the group have done in the first week to avoid the crash?
qa.a: They could have agreed on units and sizes at the start and run one short test joining their parts early.

qa.q: What was the night like for Urmila?
qa.a: It was probably tiring and stressful for Urmila; she kept rubbing her eyes and answered Rohan's "I thought we'd agreed" with a surprised "When?"

grounding: Shows an observer watching a student group find, the night before a demo, that parts built on different assumptions do not join.

passage: So, Ishita, you want to know why I now write handoff notes like essays? Okay. Last year, before my two weeks of leave, I passed the supply-order tracker at the clinic to Arun. My note said: "Check sheet, send reminders Friday, the usual." Three lines. I, Ayesha, the organised one, thought it was obvious. What I didn't write: that one supplier must be reminded by phone, never email, because their inbox is broken. That the red rows meant "on hold, don't chase". That the Friday reminder skips the clinic's own lab. All of that lived in my head; I'd done it for a year. So Arun emailed the broken inbox, chased every red row, and reminded our own lab. Nothing dangerous happened, but I came back to three annoyed people and one very apologetic Arun, who had done exactly what my note said.

qa.q: How many lines was Ayesha's handoff note?
qa.a: Three lines.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling when writing the note, and how did that change after the leave?
qa.a: Ayesha felt confident and sure it was obvious after doing the job for a year, then embarrassed on coming back to three annoyed people.

qa.q: What could Ayesha have added to the handoff?
qa.a: The phone-only supplier, what the red rows meant and that the Friday reminder skips the lab, plus a short talk-through with Arun before leaving.

qa.q: How might Arun have felt while covering the tracker?
qa.a: Arun likely felt confused and then sorry, since following the note exactly still caused trouble through no fault of Arun's own.

grounding: Shows a worker handing over a task with a brief note, assuming the successor knows background that lived only in their head.

passage:
Supervisor's note, site office, Thursday.
Raghav has spent four days on the drainage drawings Jagdish left when he moved to the Pune project. Today I watched him with three versions of the same plan open, trying to work out which one the client approved. The file names say only "final", "final2" and "use this". A pipe size is crossed out in pencil with no reason written. Raghav rang Jagdish twice; Jagdish is on site all day and didn't pick up.
Raghav chose "final2" and ordered the site levels on that basis. By evening we found the client had signed "use this". Two days of levels to redo. He sat with his head in his hands for a while, then said quietly, "I did the best with what I had." He did.
Next steps: I have booked a one-hour call with Jagdish for tomorrow and told Raghav in writing that the delay is not on him.

qa.q: Which version had the client actually signed?
qa.a: The client had signed "use this".

qa.q: What does Raghav sitting with his head in his hands suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt discouraged and frustrated at losing two days of work, even though he knew he had done the best with what he had.

qa.q: What could have prevented the lost days?
qa.a: A handoff note saying which file the client approved and why the pipe size changed, plus a short call before Jagdish moved, would have removed the guessing.

qa.q: How does the supervisor see Raghav's mistake?
qa.a: The supervisor sees it as not Raghav's fault, agreeing "He did" and putting in writing that the delay is not on him.

grounding: Shows a colleague taking over unfinished work with missing context and unclear decisions, losing time through no fault of their own.

passage:
On Tenzin's third week at the appliance company's office in Gurugram, a complaint came in: a family in Sector 45 had waited nine days for their water purifier to be installed. Tenzin sat right between the sales desk and the installation desk and heard both sides.
"Installation handles scheduling," said Kiran from sales, not looking up.
"Sales never sent us the address," said a voice from installation.
Tenzin opened the shared tracker. The order sat in a column called "handover", with no owner's name. Eleven other orders sat there too, some of them weeks old. Nobody had moved them, because each desk believed the other one would.
At lunch Tenzin showed Kiran the column. Kiran stared at the screen for a long moment, then said, "We need one name on this column, or it'll keep happening." That afternoon Kiran took the family's order herself and called them.

qa.q: How many other orders were sitting in the handover column?
qa.a: Eleven other orders sat there too, some of them weeks old.

qa.q: What might Tenzin have felt on opening the tracker after hearing both desks?
qa.a: Tenzin was likely curious after the two desks blamed each other, and then uneasy to find the family's order and eleven others with no owner's name.

qa.q: What fix did Kiran suggest, and why could it work?
qa.a: Kiran suggested putting one name on the handover column, so every stuck order has an owner instead of each desk waiting for the other.

qa.q: What is it like for the family in Sector 45?
qa.a: For the family it is nine days of waiting with nobody taking charge, while each desk points at the other.

grounding: Shows an observer noticing that work falling between two teams has no owner, with each side assuming it belongs to the other.

subtype: Written handoff with state, risks and contacts [Response]
passage:
"Got a minute, Payal? I want to walk you through the handoff doc before my leave."
"Sure, Gopika. I've got it open."
"Top section is done: the school fest posters are printed and the stage hire is confirmed."
"Okay."
"Pending is the sound check. It's booked for the fourteenth, but the hall key is with Mr Das in the admin office, not with security."
"Mr Das, admin. Noted."
"Risks: if it rains, the lawn is out and the backup is the basketball court. I've already asked the PE teacher, Mrs Rao; her number's in the contacts section."
"And the banner? It just says 'check spelling'."
"Good catch. Last year the printer spelt the chief guest's name wrong. Please check the proof before approving."
"Can I say it back? Done: posters, stage. Pending: sound check, key with Mr Das. Risk: rain, court, Mrs Rao. Banner proof."
"Perfect. Thank you for listening this carefully."
"Thank you for writing it like this. I won't have to guess anything."

qa.q: Who has the hall key?
qa.a: Mr Das in the admin office has the hall key, not security.

qa.q: How does Payal feel about the handoff, and what shows it?
qa.a: Payal feels relieved and appreciative, saying "Thank you for writing it like this. I won't have to guess anything."

qa.q: Which parts of Gopika's handoff made it work?
qa.a: Gopika wrote down what was done, what was pending, the risks and whom to contact, then walked through it on a short call where Payal said it back.

qa.q: What would change if Gopika had only sent a message saying "all sorted, see doc"?
qa.a: Payal might have missed that the key is with Mr Das or that the banner proof needs checking, and would have had to guess or chase people.

grounding: Shows a careful handoff listing what is done, pending, risky and whom to ask, confirmed with a short walk-through call.
